chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Choosing a song's key; song pluggers and sheet music
summary: Songs are published in the key that fits the average singer, and five-and-ten song demonstrators played them in any key.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The three songs are the keys what -- sometime we just find -- When you're writing a song, we just pick out a song according to how -- whatever the range of the song is. We try to get it in a range where an average singer can sing it. So when you write a song, you always pick out a song with the highest note in the song -- how the melody go. Then you put out -- The publisher will figure out what key they want to release it in. You know, print it in, so the average singer can, you know, can sing it. You know, fit the average singer, you know, do it doesn't be out of range, or something like that. That's what we always -- try to find the

Yeah. Because according to what's the highest note on the song. You know, what's the lowest note. You try to get it in a key where it fits that the average singer can sing. You know, they had (Inaudible) song pluggers in five and ten cent stores playing songs. You come in and you want to hear a song, so you -- "Got any new lead sheets today? New releases?" "Yeah." They would play for you the song. Back in those days, they would play songs for you that you could hear. "What key you got that in?" Well you say,
